Daily Double

Corvette Grand Sport vs. McLaren 12C: 2 ways to make an ordinary day worth driving.

By Nathaniel Ruiz · 14 minute read

There is a particular kind of car that ruins you for ordinary journeys. You buy it for the empty road, the long weekend and the early departure before anyone else is awake, and then you discover you want to take it everywhere: to dinner, to the office, on the entirely unnecessary trip for coffee when there is perfectly good coffee in the kitchen. The journey starts to matter as much as the destination, and sometimes a great deal more.

That is the appeal of our Daily Double, a Chevrolet Corvette Grand Sport and a McLaren 12C. In the game, the Daily Double is the square where you stop simply answering and start wagering, and that feels right here. Part 1 asked which keys I would take on a Saturday morning. This one asks what you would bet your Mondays on.

The pair are mid-engined V8s from 2 very different generations of engineering, they cost roughly the same money, and each promises the excitement of a supercar with enough civility to make using it feel reasonable. Reasonable is doing some work in that sentence, because these are still 2-seat performance cars. But the interesting question is how much of your life you could share with one, and how much more enjoyable that life might become. First, though, each deserves its own introduction.

The CorvetteChevrolet Corvette Grand Sport: enough, gloriously enough

There is a danger in calling a Corvette good value. Say it often enough and people start to hear a qualification: wonderful for the money, impressive for the badge, almost as good as something more expensive. The Grand Sport deserves to be judged on its own merits.

This is the regular Grand Sport, the rear-drive car without the Grand Sport X's electric front axle, and it starts at $88,495 with destination. Its naturally aspirated 6.7-liter V8 makes 535 hp and 520 lb-ft, delivered through an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission, and those numbers establish an identity before a single stopwatch comes out.

A big, naturally aspirated V8 still has enormous appeal. I like the idea of a car whose engine gives the whole experience its center of gravity, something substantial behind your shoulders that is worth waking up early to hear, and there is nothing apologetic about wanting that.

The Grand Sport also holds a particularly attractive place in the enthusiast imagination. It is the version chosen by someone who has thought about what they actually want to do with the car: fast roads, long drives, the occasional circuit, and a weekend away with someone who would appreciate arriving without needing a recovery period. That breadth is the point.

The joy of a capable road car is being able to settle into it. You start to trust its responses, make smaller corrections and enjoy the road as one continuous piece of driving, where a good corner becomes the beginning of the next. Eventually you stop itemizing what the car is doing and start appreciating how naturally it all comes together. For me, that is the Grand Sport's most compelling promise: the chance to become fluent in something extraordinarily capable.

The first road tests back that up, with one honest caveat. Motor Trend came away impressed by how much it involves its driver, and Car and Driver liked the way its adaptive dampers keep the body tied down while still soaking up bumps. Edmunds, which bought one for its long-term fleet, was cooler. It found the Grand Sport accelerates and stops almost exactly like the cheaper Stingray, and that its steering tells you less than you would like. Those are their verdicts rather than a back-to-back drive of our own, but the disagreement is worth knowing before you sign anything.

Then the numbers make their entrance. Car and Driver's car, a $142,380 example with the Z52 Track Performance package and Cup 2 R tires, ran to 60 mph in 2.7 seconds and through the quarter-mile in 11.0 seconds at 123 mph, and it pulled 1.18 g. Those results belong to that specification and can't simply be handed to every Grand Sport in the showroom.

For this article's road-going brief, Edmunds' car is the more relevant one: a $112,605 example with the $3,500 Z52 Sport Performance package and Michelin Pilot Sport 4S tires, which recorded 3.3 seconds, 11.4 seconds at 119.3 mph and 1.07 g. Different equipment and different test methods explain most of the gap, and even the less spectacular set describes a very serious car.

Which brings us to the question that follows the Grand Sport around: do you need more car than this? I don't think so. You might want more, because enthusiasts are exceptionally talented at wanting more, but for road driving, touring and an occasional track day, the Grand Sport makes an imposing case for being enough, and for making enough feel rather magnificent.

And if Edmunds is right that a $73,495 Stingray runs nearly the same numbers, then the Grand Sport's extra money buys the wider body, the bigger tires and the look. Plenty of buyers will call that money well spent.

The McLarenMcLaren 12C: the engineering is the romance

The McLaren creates a different kind of anticipation. A 12C has the proportions, the upward-swinging doors and the sense of purpose to make simply walking up to it feel like the beginning of something. It asks you to step into a different environment, built around a carbon-fiber passenger cell and a driving position the road testers of the day singled out for praise.

Its shape appeals to me because it seems comfortable with itself. The drama is already there in the way the car sits and in the machinery it carries, and I can imagine its owner pausing for one more look before going inside.

For this comparison, the target is the 616-hp car: a 2013 model, or an earlier one with the factory upgrade documented. McLaren gave existing owners the extra power free of charge, along with drivetrain and usability improvements, so a car's registration year alone can't tell you which specification it has.

The twin-turbocharged 3.8-liter V8 sends its power to the rear wheels through a 7-speed dual-clutch gearbox, and its appeal is a different flavor from the Corvette's. Here the prospect is the gathering force of the boost, the anticipation of another gear and the slow realization that the car contains far more performance than an ordinary road could ever sensibly reveal.

On their makers' own best-case numbers, the 2 cars make the point beautifully. The Corvette reaches 60 mph first, a quarter-second ahead, but by the end of the quarter-mile the McLaren is long gone, crossing the line 12 mph faster. One is built to leap, the other to keep pulling. Car and Driver's own estimate for the 2014 coupe, 2.9 seconds to 60 mph and a 10.7-second quarter-mile, lands right beside McLaren's claim.

But the suspension is what makes the 12C such a fascinating part of this story. Its hydraulically linked dampers control body roll without conventional anti-roll bars, and test after test remarked on how it held the body flat and still rode gently. Motor Trend's first test admired the precision of the steering and the way the car floated over freeway expansion joints, although that test drove the earlier 592-hp car, so its acceleration figures don't belong to the upgraded one.

I find that engineering deeply romantic. Think about the ambition involved: build a car this fast, then give its driver a reason to enjoy the miles when speed is irrelevant. There is a particular pleasure in discovering that something exotic can also be considerate, that the road doesn't have to be perfect, that a long journey might be part of the attraction, and that the person beside you could enjoy the trip for reasons beyond generously indulging your enthusiasm.

Edmunds, reviewing the 2013 car, praised the handling, the driving position and the gearbox, and counted commuting comfort among its strengths. It also wondered whether all that polish left enough emotional theater. That criticism interests me. Some people want a supercar to make its presence felt at every opportunity, while others find real character in a machine that makes demanding work feel unusually composed. The 12C offers a way to love the thinking as much as the spectacle.

The moneyNow put them on the same shopping list

The overlap in purchase price is real, and it is closer than you might think. CLASSIC.COM's benchmark for 12C coupes, built from completed sales, sits at about $91,400. Dealers ask more: the 9 priced 12C coupes on Autotrader today run from $99,995 to $120,886, with a median of $113,201. That is $596 more than Edmunds paid for its Grand Sport, which is about as close to the same money as 2 cars this different will ever get. One more thing from those listings: every one of those coupes is a 2012, so the paperwork for the free 616-hp upgrade is the first thing to ask for.

That makes this a comparison of 2 routes into ownership: a new car engineered to deliver enormous capability today, and an older exotic whose depreciation has brought a very different kind of machinery within reach. A 2014 12C started at $241,900 with destination, about $344,300 in 2026 dollars, so today's buyer pays somewhere between a quarter and a third of what that car once asked. They don't need to be equivalent in every respect for that to be an interesting decision.

The recipeApples, oranges and the recipe

People often dismiss a comparison like this one as apples and oranges. Fine. Both are excellent ingredients, and the useful question is what you are making.

If your recipe calls for frequent use, weekends away, modern convenience and the occasional track day without reorganizing your whole relationship with the car, the Grand Sport becomes enormously attractive. I would choose its equipment around the miles I would actually drive, rather than chase a headline grip figure on tires that might not suit them. If your recipe starts with the desire to own a McLaren, to experience that cabin, those doors and that chassis thinking, and the particular satisfaction of making an extraordinary object part of your life, then the 12C answers something the Corvette was never required to answer.

Neither owner has misunderstood the assignment. The person choosing the Corvette may have spent years dreaming about one, and the person choosing the McLaren may have studied every maintenance invoice before buying. Passion and judgment are available on both sides of the garage, and the only difference is the balance of ingredients.

The tourTouring is where the idea becomes interesting

Imagine leaving before sunrise with an overnight bag and no obligation to be home that evening. The best touring companion makes you want to keep going. It gives you a reason to leave the highway when the interesting road appears, then enough comfort to rejoin it when the weather closes in or the day grows long.

That is the version of supercar ownership I find most appealing: a machine that becomes part of a memory rather than simply the subject of a photograph. Both of these cars deserve to be judged on that basis. Neither needs a racetrack to justify every mile, and neither should be measured only by how often its owner goes near a limit.

There is reward in a well-timed overtake, an accurately judged bend, or simply arriving with the urge to drive again tomorrow. The grand tour has always been as much about appetite as endurance.

The MondayAnd then Monday comes

The daily-driver question is personal. Your parking space, your driveway, your traffic, your luggage and your tolerance for attention matter far more than anyone else's claim that a supercar is perfectly usable.

The McLaren's doors and its carbon tub deserve a physical trial in the space where you actually intend to park. For 2013, McLaren replaced the 12C's fussy touch-sensor door releases with a simple button, and a lift system to raise the nose over steep driveways became an option, so confirm whether the car you are looking at has one and that it works. Details like these make a real difference to how an exotic fits into ordinary routines, and at 75.2 inches wide and 47.4 inches tall, the 12C is a lot of car to thread into a garage.

The Corvette deserves the same honesty. A low, wide performance car still has to negotiate your daily life, and the badge doesn't make every driveway friendly or every parking space generous.

Then separate comfort from the cost of ownership. An older McLaren can ride beautifully and still need a budget appropriate to its machinery and its condition, because a lower purchase price doesn't make it any less complex than it was new. A specialist's inspection, documented updates, access to service and a credible maintenance fund all belong beside the dream.

Running costs are one place they meet. The EPA rates the 12C at 15 mpg in the city and 22 on the highway, and the Grand Sport at 15 and 23, so the fuel bills are a tie. A new Corvette offers a different starting point, including a new-car warranty on its own terms. That doesn't make tires free or every repair convenient, but it changes the ownership math rather than eliminating it. The right car is the one you will feel comfortable using, financially as well as physically.

The wagerWhich recipe would I make?

If I were choosing one car to use often, to take away for a weekend, enjoy on a quiet road and sometimes drive to work, I would begin with the Grand Sport. I keep returning to how complete its proposition seems. There is enough engine to make every departure an occasion and enough capability to leave me little reason to wish for more, so I could spend my energy choosing the road and learning the car.

But I could understand buying the McLaren without needing to be persuaded by another performance figure. Some purchases are about the experience you have wanted for years, and provided the particular car and the ownership budget survive scrutiny, that is a perfectly legitimate reason. There is no spreadsheet cell for the feeling of opening your garage and finding the thing you never quite believed you would own.

The Grand Sport appeals to my desire to go everywhere. The 12C appeals to my desire to make everywhere feel a little less ordinary.

Both offer the ingredients for a life with more driving in it, and both can be loved for exactly what they are. So, how much are you wagering?

If the answer is everything, make it a true Daily Double. In 2014 the 12C made way for the 650S: the same carbon tub and the same V8, turned up to 641 hp, wearing a face borrowed from the P1. It is the better car on paper and the pricier one used, at about $139,000 for a 2016 coupe by CarGurus' reckoning, roughly $25,000 past the 12C's asking prices and well past this budget. That is the square for the player who wants to bet it all. For the rest of us, tell me the recipe you want to make, and then we can choose the keys.
